newsitem.title: USA: Farm trade concerns a big issue in China entering WTO.
newsitem.headline: Farm trade concerns a big issue in China entering WTO.

text.p: U.S. officials said Wednesday that farm trade issues will be a key factor in whether China joins the World Trade Organisation, and denied charges the White House was giving short shrift to unresolved agricultural disputes between Washington and Beijing.

"We know what the issues are in agriculture very well, and so does the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative)" said Paul Drazek, senior trade adviser to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman. "We've been working with them very closely."

"Agriculture trade barriers to China are one of the most difficult and pernicious to solve," said a spokesman for the Trade Representative's Office. "We are interested in working actively with USDA on this."

Agricultural groups and lawmakers representing rural areas have launched an aggressive campaign to make sure farm interests do not get pushed aside in U.S.-China talks, in favour of other big-ticket sectors like telecommunications or computers.

A letter sent to President Clinton earlier this month from a group of farm state senators, including Senate Agriculture Committee chairman Richard Lugar, an Indiana Republican, urged Clinton to make increasing agricultural exports to China a top priority and detailed a list of concerns to be addressed in negotiations with China.

At a meeting of the agriculture committee Wednesday, Lugar said he was disappointed that agriculture did not receive sufficient discussion at last year's WTO ministerial meeting in Singapore, and ranking minority committee member Sen. Tom Harkin, Democrat of Iowa declared, "Our trade office has got to focus on agriculture ... our trade office is giving us short shrift."
The worry that agricultural issues are not being adequately attended to in talks with China has been voiced by several major farm groups.

"Our negotiators on WTO have to be negotiating with agricultural officials in China, and we don't see any sign of that," said Barbara Spangler, director of government relations for the American Farm Bureau Federation. "We have to get USTR involved in this."

Agricultural officials list a wide array of concerns with China, ranging from high import duties on a broad spectrum of food items and bulk commodities, to unscientifically-based restrictions on imports of U.S. grain, produce and meats.
U.S. trade officials contend that they are well aware of the problems and are actively addressing them.

A working group of officials from the Agriculture Department, the Trade Representative's Office and other agencies has been formed to study U.S.-China agricultural issues, Agriculture Department's Drazek said, and "will be meeting frequently in the weeks and months to come."
Administration officials will be travelling to China later this week for bilateral trade talks, and agricultural issues will be discussed, said a U.S. trade official.

"We are still trying to determine whether in fact we can get in a position later this year to develop an (WTO) agreement that is commercially meaningful for the U.S. across all industries, and agriculture is one of the key sectors," said the official.
